title: Why Aquila and Priscilla were in Corinth
summary: Luke says the couple had 'recently come from Italy, because Claudius had ordered all Jews to leave Rome'. Suetonius records an expulsion of the Jews from Rome under Claudius, and gives a reason: constant disturbances 'at the instigation of Chrestus'.
body: Acts 18:2 gives the expulsion in passing, as the reason a tentmaker and his wife Paul meets have newly arrived from Italy. Suetonius, writing around AD 120, says of Claudius: Iudaeos impulsore Chresto assidue tumultuantis Roma expulit, 'because the Jews were constantly making disturbances at the instigation of Chrestus, he expelled them from Rome'.

Chrestus was an ordinary name, and Suetonius's sentence makes Chrestus the instigator. Tertullian, ≈AD 197, complains that Romans say 'Chrestianus' for Christianus, and Orosius, in the fifth century, quotes Suetonius's sentence as 'inpulsore Christo', at the instigation of Christ: he read it as disputes over Jesus. Dixon Slingerland (1997) argues instead that Chrestus was a man in Rome, a name found often enough in inscriptions; Erich Gruen, reviewing him, writes that the passage 'implies that Chrestus the impulsor was in Rome' and that the Christian reading cannot be saved 'by postulating Suetonius' ignorance', while calling Slingerland's own candidate, an adviser of Claudius, 'highly speculative'.

Orosius puts the expulsion in Claudius' ninth year, AD 49, citing Josephus for it, but no such passage is in Josephus's surviving works. Cassius Dio, describing AD 41, says Claudius did not expel the Jews but forbade them to meet. AD 49 agrees with Acts, where Paul reaches Corinth before Gallio's proconsulship (see the Gallio card), but Orosius, writing nearly four centuries later, is the only source that gives the year.

In Acts Paul stays and works with the couple, 'for they were tentmakers by trade' (18:3). Paul later sends greetings from the church in their house at Ephesus (1 Corinthians 16:19) and to the church in their house at Rome (Romans 16:3-5).

title: Two accounts of the death of Herod Agrippa I
summary: Acts and Josephus describe the same death in the same city: the king in royal dress, a crowd hailing him as a god, a sudden agony in the abdomen, and a death some days later.
body: Acts 12:21-23: on an appointed day Herod puts on his royal robes, takes his seat and addresses the people; they shout 'the voice of a god and not of a man'; he is struck down 'because he did not give God the glory', is eaten by worms and dies.

Josephus, Antiquities 19.343-350, gives far more detail. Agrippa is at Caesarea for games in the emperor's honour. On the second day he enters the theatre early in a garment woven entirely of silver, which catches the rising sun so brightly that onlookers are afraid to look at him. Flatterers call out that he is a god. He does not rebuke them, and immediately a pain seizes his stomach; he is carried out, suffers for five days and dies, aged fifty-four, in the seventh year of his reign — AD 44.

Josephus has the silver robe, the omen of an owl and the five days; Acts has the Tyre and Sidon embassy and the angel. Both have the city, the royal dress, the acclamation as divine, the king's failure to refuse it, the illness and the death. Ben Witherington reads the two as independent accounts, neither writer using the other.

Witherington notes that 'eaten by worms' (skolekobrotos) is a stock phrase in Greek and Jewish writing for the death of a tyrant. Josephus says only 'a pain in his belly, violent from the start'. Neither account gives more than that, so any modern diagnosis, from a ruptured appendix to intestinal parasites, is a conjecture of its proposer's.

title: The census problem in Luke 2
summary: Luke dates the birth of Jesus by a registration 'when Quirinius was governor of Syria'. The census Quirinius is known to have run took place in AD 6, ten years after Herod the Great died on one reckoning of his death and seven on the other. This card sets out the difficulty and the answers proposed, and gives no verdict between them.
body: Luke 1:5 and Matthew 2:1 put the birth in the reign of Herod the Great, whose death is reckoned to 4 BC or to 1 BC (see the card on dating Herod's death). Luke 2:2 dates the registration to Quirinius' governorship of Syria. Josephus describes Quirinius arriving in Syria after Augustus deposed Herod's son Archelaus and annexed Judea, to assess the new province for tax — reckoned by Josephus as thirty-seven years after Actium, which is AD 6. That census provoked the revolt of Judas the Galilean, which Luke himself refers to in Acts 5:37. The two dates are about ten years apart on the 4 BC reckoning of Herod's death, seven on the 1 BC.

Brown surveys the proposals. (1) Translate prote as 'before': 'this registration was before Quirinius was governor', the reading I. Howard Marshall defends. (2) An earlier commission: on this proposal Quirinius held authority in the East around 7-6 BC, alongside the legate Sentius Saturninus, and conducted a registration then. The Lapis Tiburtinus, an inscription naming an unidentified official who governed Syria twice, is brought in for it, but it does not name Quirinius. (3) A long registration: Augustus ordered an empire-wide enrolment carried out province by province over years, completed in Judea under Quirinius. (4) Luke is mistaken on the date, Brown's own conclusion.

Josephus attests the AD 6 census under Quirinius. No source outside Luke tells of a census of Judea under Herod. Each of the four proposals is a reconstruction, and this card is marked as an interpretation for that reason.

title: Which books are scripture? The churches' four answers
summary: Every church reads the 66 books. They differ over the Jewish writings of the last centuries BC and the first AD that the Hebrew Bible does not contain: Catholics count seven of them and the Greek parts of Esther and Daniel as scripture, Orthodox churches more, the Ethiopian church more again, including 1 Enoch and Jubilees; Protestants read them, if at all, as useful but not scripture.
body: Jesus speaks of 'the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms' (Luke 24:44). Sirach's translator, who came to Egypt 'in the thirty-eighth year' of King Euergetes (≈132 BC, taking the king to be Ptolemy VIII), writes of what was handed down 'by the law and the prophets, and by the others that have followed in their steps'. Josephus, writing about AD 95, counts 'only twenty-two books' held divine, and says the histories written after Artaxerxes are not 'esteemed of the like authority'. None of these names the books one by one.

The Greek-speaking churches read their Old Testament in the Septuagint, which also held books the Hebrew Bible does not: Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch, the Maccabees and longer forms of Esther and Daniel. The councils of North Africa (Hippo 393, repeated at Carthage in 419) listed Tobit, Judith, two books of Maccabees and 'five books of Solomon'. Augustine, who wrote of the same list, says Wisdom and Ecclesiasticus (Sirach) 'are ascribed to Solomon from a certain resemblance of style'. The Council of Trent (1546) made the Catholic list binding: those books and Baruch, with every book received 'entire with all their parts', the Greek parts of Esther and Daniel among them.

The Orthodox Synod of Jerusalem (1672) named Wisdom, Judith, Tobit, Susanna, Bel and the Dragon, the Maccabees and Sirach as genuine parts of scripture, refusing them the name Apocrypha. Orthodox editions differ on 1 Esdras, 3 and 4 Maccabees, the Prayer of Manasseh and Psalm 151, and Slavonic Bibles add 2 Esdras. The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church counts 81 books, among them 1 Enoch and Jubilees, which survive whole only in Ge'ez. Jude 14–15 quotes 1 Enoch 1:9, and Aramaic fragments of 1 Enoch were found at Qumran.

The Reformers kept the books but set them apart. The 1611 King James Bible printed them as the Apocrypha between Malachi and Matthew, and the Church of England's Article VI lists them as books the Church 'doth read for example of life and instruction of manners; but yet doth it not apply them to establish any doctrine'. The Westminster Confession (1646) went further: they are 'no part of the canon of the Scripture', not to be 'made use of' otherwise 'than other human writings'. The BSB, the translation this reader uses, does not include them.

It has been written that a rabbinic council at Jamnia (Yavneh), around AD 90, closed the Hebrew canon and shut these books out. Jack P. Lewis, examining the evidence (1964), found nothing to support a canon-closing council there. The Mishnah records a dispute over whether the Song of Songs and Ecclesiastes 'defile the hands', settled by a tradition from 'the day when they appointed Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah head of the academy'; it rules on those two books and gives no list.

Here the books beyond the 66 have their own section of the book list, and on the Links circle their own arc, set between the Testaments where the 1611 King James put them. Each is marked with the churches that read it. The text is the World English Bible's or R. H. Charles's, not the BSB, so there is no interlinear or word study for them.

title: John the Baptist in Josephus
summary: Josephus tells of John, 'called the Baptist', a good man who urged the Jews to virtue and baptism, and whom Herod Antipas killed at the fortress of Machaerus for fear his following would rise — a second account of the Gospels' story, with a different motive.
body: Josephus's Antiquities, written in Rome about AD 93, describes Antipas's war with Aretas of Nabataea and adds: 'some of the Jews thought that the destruction of Herod's army came from God, and that very justly, as a punishment of what he did against John, that was called the Baptist: for Herod slew him, who was a good man, and commanded the Jews to exercise virtue … and so to come to baptism.' John was 'sent a prisoner … to Macherus … and was there put to death'.

The Gospels say John was arrested for condemning Antipas's marriage to Herodias (Mark 6:17-18). Josephus says Antipas feared that John's influence 'might put it into his power and inclination to raise a rebellion'. In Josephus's account the marriage to Herodias is also what set Aretas against Antipas, in the war that followed.

Josephus gives names the Gospels leave out. He names Machaerus, the fortress east of the Dead Sea, as the place John died. Herodias's daughter, unnamed in Mark, was Salome, who later married Philip the tetrarch. And Herodias's first husband, whom Mark calls Philip, Josephus calls Herod, a son of Herod the Great by the high priest Simon's daughter. Whether he bore both names is not known.
The passage says nothing of Jesus, and its account of John's baptism differs from the Gospels'.

title: King Aretas: why his governor watched Damascus's gates
summary: Paul escaped Damascus in a basket because 'the governor under King Aretas' was guarding the city. Aretas IV of Nabataea was the father of the wife Herod Antipas divorced for Herodias, and Josephus tells how he went to war with Antipas over it.
body: Josephus: Antipas 'had married the daughter of Aretas', but fell in love with Herodias and agreed to divorce her. She learned of it, fled to her father, and 'Aretas made this the first occasion of his enmity between him and Herod'. In the war that followed, 'all Herod's army was destroyed'. Tiberius ordered Vitellius, the governor of Syria, to march on Aretas, but news of the emperor's death (AD 37) reached Vitellius on the way and he called the army home.

2 Corinthians 11:32 says his ethnarch 'secured the city of the Damascenes in order to arrest me'; Acts 9 says the Jews watched the gates. Galatians 1:17 adds that Paul had gone 'into Arabia' before returning to Damascus.

Aretas IV's death is dated ≈AD 40, from his dated coins and inscriptions. If that date holds, Paul's escape, and with it his conversion three years earlier (Galatians 1:18), was no later. How a Nabataean official came to hold the gates of a Roman city is not known.

title: The death of James, 'the brother of Jesus, who was called Christ'
summary: Josephus records that in AD 62, between two Roman governors, the high priest Ananus convened the Sanhedrin and had 'the brother of Jesus, who was called Christ, whose name was James' stoned — and was deposed for it after three months.
body: Acts shows James leading the Jerusalem church (15:13-21; 21:18), and Paul calls him 'the Lord's brother' (Galatians 1:19). Josephus tells how he died. When the governor Festus died in office, and before his successor Albinus arrived, the young high priest Ananus 'assembled the sanhedrim of judges, and brought before them the brother of Jesus, who was called Christ, whose name was James, and some others … and delivered them to be stoned'.

The fairest-minded citizens, Josephus says, objected, and some went to meet Albinus on the road to complain that Ananus had no right to convene the court without the governor. King Agrippa II removed Ananus after three months. The year, AD 62, comes from the governors' dates: Festus is the governor of Acts 24:27-26:32.

The passage names Jesus only to identify James, as the one 'who was called Christ'. Eusebius preserves a later and fuller account by Hegesippus, in which James is thrown from the temple and clubbed to death.

James had not always followed his brother. During the ministry 'even His own brothers did not believe in Him' (John 7:5), and his family once came 'to take custody of Him, saying, “He is out of His mind”' (Mark 3:21). Paul's list of witnesses has the risen Jesus appear 'to James' (1 Corinthians 15:7), whom Eusebius takes to be this James, and within a few years he is one of the church's 'pillars' in Jerusalem (Galatians 1:19; 2:9). In Hegesippus's account (≈AD 170), the scribes stand him on the temple's pinnacle and ask him to turn the Passover crowds from Jesus; he answers that Jesus 'sits in heaven at the right hand of the great Power', and they throw him down and stone him. Josephus's account is the earlier, and has no such scene.

title: Theudas and Judas: Gamaliel's examples, and a dating problem
summary: Gamaliel cites Theudas and then Judas the Galilean as movements that came to nothing. Josephus tells of a Theudas too, but under the governor Fadus, about AD 45 — a decade after Gamaliel speaks, and forty years after Judas.
body: In Acts 5:36-37 Gamaliel says: 'Some time ago Theudas rose up, claiming to be somebody, and about four hundred men joined him. He was killed … After him, Judas the Galilean appeared in the days of the census.' Josephus tells of Judas's revolt against the census of AD 6.

Josephus's Theudas is a 'magician' who, 'while Fadus was procurator of Judea' (≈AD 44–46, from the order of governors Josephus gives), led a crowd to the Jordan promising to part it. Roman cavalry killed many, and Theudas's head was taken to Jerusalem. The next paragraph mentions the crucifixion of 'the sons of Judas of Galilee' — so Josephus names Theudas and then Judas, in the order of Acts, though Judas's revolt was much earlier.

The difficulty is old. Origen, around AD 248, followed Acts and put 'a certain Theudas … before the birth of Christ'. Those who follow Origen take Gamaliel to mean another, earlier Theudas, perhaps one of the rebels in the unrest after Herod's death. Richard Pervo, who holds that Luke used Josephus, takes Luke to have placed Josephus's Theudas too early. The two accounts also differ on numbers: Acts has about four hundred followers, Josephus 'a great part of the people'.

title: 'Aren't you the Egyptian?' — the prophet of the Mount of Olives
summary: The Roman commander who arrested Paul took him for 'the Egyptian who incited a rebellion and led four thousand of the Assassins into the wilderness'. Josephus tells of the same man: under Felix he led a crowd to the Mount of Olives promising Jerusalem's walls would fall, and escaped when the Romans attacked.
body: Josephus has the story twice. In the Jewish War: 'an Egyptian false prophet … got together thirty thousand men that were deluded by him; these he led round about from the wilderness to the mount which was called the Mount of Olives', meaning to take Jerusalem. Felix's soldiers routed them and 'the Egyptian ran away, with a few others'. In the Antiquities he promised that 'at his command, the walls of Jerusalem would fall down', and Felix's troops killed four hundred and took two hundred alive; 'the Egyptian himself escaped out of the fight, but did not appear any more'.
Josephus says he escaped and 'did not appear any more'; in Acts the commander takes Paul for him. The figures differ: Acts has 4,000, the War 30,000.

Acts calls his followers sikarioi, 'the Assassins' in the BSB. Josephus describes the sicarii, named for the short dagger (sica) they hid under their clothes, as arising under Felix. They stabbed opponents in the festival crowds, and their first victim was the high priest Jonathan.

title: Agabus's famine, 'under Claudius'
summary: Acts says Agabus foretold a great famine, which came 'under Claudius', and the church at Antioch sent relief to Judea by Barnabas and Saul. Josephus describes a famine in Judea under the governors Fadus and Tiberius Alexander, which Queen Helena of Adiabene relieved with grain from Egypt.
body: Luke adds, 'This happened under Claudius' (AD 41–54). Josephus: 'Under these procurators' (Fadus and Tiberius Alexander, ≈AD 44–48 from the order of governors he gives) 'that great famine happened in Judea, in which queen Helena bought corn in Egypt at a great expense, and distributed it to those that were in want.'

Helena, a convert to Judaism and the mother of the king of Adiabene in northern Mesopotamia, was in Jerusalem when the famine struck, 'and many people died for want of what was necessary'. She sent servants to Alexandria for grain and to Cyprus for dried figs; her son sent money. In Acts the Antioch disciples also sent relief, each 'according to his ability' (11:29).

Acts says the famine would be 'over the whole world', meaning the Roman world. Josephus speaks of Judea; Suetonius says that in Claudius's reign there was 'a scarcity of grain because of long-continued droughts' at Rome. Neither describes one famine across the empire at once.

title: Felix and Drusilla
summary: Felix listened to Paul with 'his wife Drusilla, who was a Jewess'. Josephus says she was the daughter of King Agrippa I, persuaded by a Cypriot magician to leave her husband, the king of Emesa, for Felix. Tacitus said Felix wielded 'the power of a king with all the instincts of a slave'.
body: Josephus: 'While Felix was procurator of Judea, he saw this Drusilla, and fell in love with her … and he sent to her a person whose name was Simon, one of his friends; a Jew he was, and by birth a Cypriot, and one who pretended to be a magician', to persuade her to leave her husband Azizus. She married Felix, 'to transgress the laws of her forefathers'. Their son Agrippa later died in the eruption of Vesuvius.

She was the daughter of the Herod Agrippa of Acts 12, and the sister of Agrippa II and Bernice, before whom Paul spoke two years later (Acts 25:13-26:32). When Paul spoke to Felix 'about righteousness, self-control, and the judgment to come' (24:25), he was speaking to a couple whose marriage, in Josephus's words, was 'to transgress the laws of her forefathers'.

Felix was a freedman, the brother of Claudius's minister Pallas. Tacitus says he 'practised every kind of cruelty and lust, wielding the power of king with all the instincts of a slave', and Suetonius that he became 'the husband of three queens'. Tacitus's Drusilla is a different woman, a granddaughter of Antony and Cleopatra, so Felix married two Drusillas. Acts says he hoped Paul would offer him a bribe (24:26).

title: Annas: high priest, and father of high priests
summary: Jesus was taken 'first to Annas', though Caiaphas was high priest. Josephus tells who Annas was: (Ananus son of Seth) had been high priest himself, and five of his sons held the office after him — a family that kept power while Rome appointed and removed its priests.
body: Josephus records that Quirinius appointed 'Ananus, the son of Seth, to be high priest' in AD 6, and that the governor Gratus deposed him (≈AD 15). Gratus then made and unmade three high priests in as many years — one of them Annas's son Eleazar — before 'Joseph Caiaphas was made his successor'. Caiaphas lasted until Vitellius removed him, about AD 36, and appointed 'Jonathan the son of Ananus'.

Of the elder Ananus, Josephus says that 'he had five sons who had all performed the office of a high priest to God … which had never happened to any other of our high priests'. The youngest, also Ananus, is the high priest who had James killed in AD 62.

John alone says Caiaphas was Annas's son-in-law (18:13). Luke dates John the Baptist's ministry 'during the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas' (3:2), and Acts 4:6 calls Annas 'the high priest' years after Josephus has him deposed.

title: 'If you suffer as a Christian': Pliny's trials in Bithynia
summary: 1 Peter writes to Christians in provinces including Bithynia, who may 'suffer as a Christian'. Pliny, governing Bithynia ≈AD 110–112, asked Trajan whether 'the very profession of Christianity' was punishable, and executed those who would not deny the name.
body: The word 'Christian' occurs only three times in the New Testament: the disciples were first called so at Antioch (Acts 11:26), Agrippa uses it (26:28), and 1 Peter 4:16 tells readers not to be ashamed if they suffer 'as a Christian'. The letter is addressed to 'Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia' (1:1).

Pliny the Younger governed Bithynia and Pontus for Trajan ≈AD 110–112, the dates resting on his correspondence with the emperor. He wrote asking how to deal with Christians: 'whether the very profession of Christianity, unattended with any criminal act, or only the crimes themselves inherent in the profession are punishable'. Meanwhile he asked the accused three times whether they were Christians and had those who persisted executed, sending Roman citizens to Rome.

Those who had left the faith told him they used to 'meet on a stated day before it was light, and address a form of prayer to Christ, as to a divinity', binding themselves by oath not to steal or commit adultery, and later met to eat 'a harmless meal'. He tortured two slave women 'who were said to officiate', and found only 'an absurd and extravagant superstition'. Trajan replied that Christians were not to be sought out, but if accused and convicted must be punished unless they recanted.

Pliny's letter does not date 1 Peter. It records that in Bithynia, one of the provinces 1 Peter addresses, Pliny executed those who held to the name while still asking whether the name alone was a crime.

title: Why 1 John 5:7 is shorter than in the King James
summary: The KJV reads 'there are three that bear record in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost: and these three are one'. Those words, the Johannine Comma, are not in any early Greek manuscript of 1 John; they are first found in Latin Bibles, and entered the printed Greek text in 1522. The BSB leaves them out.
body: The BSB's 1 John 5:7-8 reads: 'For there are three that testify: the Spirit, the water, and the blood — and these three are in agreement.' The King James adds a heavenly witness between them: 'the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost: and these three are one. And there are three that bear witness in earth'.

Metzger sets out the evidence. The Greek codices of the fourth and fifth centuries, Sinaiticus, Vaticanus and Alexandrinus, do not have the words, and the Greek writers of the early church do not quote them, though they argued at length over the Trinity. They are first found in Latin, from the fourth century on, and spread through the Latin Vulgate. The few Greek manuscripts that have them are late.

Erasmus left them out of the first two editions of his Greek New Testament (1516, 1519) and put them into the third (1522), on the evidence of a Greek manuscript produced in his own day. Later printed editions, and from them the King James, kept them.
Metzger's edition of the Greek leaves them out, as does the BSB.

title: The letters some doubted: James, 2 Peter, 2–3 John, Jude
summary: Writing about AD 325, Eusebius sorted the New Testament books into those every church accepted and those 'disputed … nevertheless recognized by many': James, Jude, 2 Peter, and 2 and 3 John. All five were in the canon lists before the end of the century.
body: Eusebius's Church History sets out the state of the question in his day: 'Among the disputed writings, which are nevertheless recognized by many, are extant the so-called epistle of James and that of Jude, also the second epistle of Peter, and those that are called the second and third of John, whether they belong to the evangelist or to another person of the same name.' The Gospels, Acts, Paul's letters, 1 Peter and 1 John he lists as accepted by all.

Jerome, about AD 392, gives the reasons he had heard: 2 Peter, 'on account of its difference from the first in style, is considered by many not to be by him'; James 'is claimed by some to have been published by some one else under his name'; Jude, because it quotes 1 Enoch, 'is rejected by many'. Of 2 and 3 John, Eusebius's own words above give the doubt: whether they are by the evangelist 'or to another person of the same name'. Eusebius also wavers over Revelation, listing it both as accepted 'if it really seem proper' and among the rejected.

The disputes did not leave these books out. Athanasius's Easter letter of 367 lists the 27 books of the New Testament, including 'of Peter, two; of John, three; after these, one of Jude', and the councils of North Africa in the 390s and 419 do the same. 2 Peter itself speaks of 'all his letters', Paul's, and of people who distort them 'as they do the rest of the Scriptures' (3:16).

title: Who is 'the elder'?
summary: 2 and 3 John are from 'the elder', unnamed. Irenaeus, about AD 180, quotes 2 John as the work of the Lord's disciple John. But Papias, early in the second century, named two Johns among his sources — the apostle and 'the presbyter John' — and Jerome reports that some credited these two letters to the second.
body: Neither letter names its writer; both open 'The elder' (ho presbyteros). Their language is close to 1 John and the Gospel of John. Irenaeus quotes 2 John's 'many deceivers' as written by the Lord's 'disciple, in his Epistle already mentioned', the author of 1 John.

Papias, bishop of Hierapolis, wrote that he used to ask what 'Andrew or what Peter said, or … James, or by John, or by Matthew … and what things Aristion and the presbyter John, the disciples of the Lord, say'. Eusebius, quoting him, noticed that John is 'twice enumerated', once among the apostles and once after Aristion and 'distinctly called a presbyter', and added that there were two tombs at Ephesus each called John's.

Jerome, around 392, says the two letters 'are said to be the work of John the presbyter, to the memory of whom another sepulchre is shown at Ephesus to the present day'. Eusebius lists them among the disputed books for this reason. Whether Papias's 'presbyter John' is a second man or the apostle under an older title is itself debated.

title: 'The Song of Songs is the holy of holies'
summary: The Mishnah records rabbis disputing whether the Song of Songs and Ecclesiastes 'defile the hands' — the rabbinic test of a holy book. Rabbi Akiva defended the Song: 'all the writings are holy but the Song of Songs is the holy of holies'.
body: A scroll of Scripture, by rabbinic rule, made the hands that touched it ritually unclean, a mark of its holiness. Mishnah Yadayim 3:5 asks which books do. 'All the Holy Scriptures defile the hands. The Song of Songs and Kohelet (Ecclesiastes) defile the hands.' Then the dissent: Rabbi Judah says the Song does but Ecclesiastes is disputed; Rabbi Yose says the reverse.

Rabbi Akiva (died ≈AD 135, after the Bar Kokhba revolt) answers: 'Far be it! No man in Israel disputed that the Song of Songs … does not defile the hands. For the whole world is not as worthy as the day on which the Song of Songs was given to Israel; for all the writings are holy but the Song of Songs is the holy of holies. If they had a dispute, they had a dispute only about Kohelet.' Ben Azzai reports a ruling for both books on the day Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah was made head of the academy.
The Mishnah does not say why either book was questioned. It records the dispute and Ben Azzai's report that both were ruled to defile the hands.

title: When did Job live? The Talmud's answers
summary: The book of Job names no king and gives no date. The Talmud collects the rabbis' guesses — Job lived in the time of Moses, of the spies, of Jacob, of the return from exile — and one sage's view that 'Job never existed … his story was a parable'.
body: Job is set 'in the land of Uz' (1:1), outside Israel, among people Genesis connects with Esau and Aram. Job offers burnt offerings himself for his children (1:5), and his wealth is counted in flocks and herds (1:3), as Abraham's and Jacob's are in Genesis.

The Babylonian Talmud (Bava Batra 15a) records the debate. A baraita says Moses wrote 'the book of Job', and Rabbi Levi bar Lahma that 'Job lived in the time of Moses'; Rava, at the time of the spies; others in Jacob's day, or among the exiles who returned under the Second Temple, with a house of study in Tiberias. One sage said before Rabbi Shmuel bar Nahmani: 'Job never existed and was never created … Rather, his story was a parable', and was answered that a parable would not give the man's name and city.
Ezekiel names him with Noah and Daniel as righteous men (14:14, 20), and James cites 'Job's perseverance' (5:11). Whether the book is history, parable or both is a question the rabbis already asked.

title: What Edom did when Jerusalem fell
summary: Obadiah condemns Edom for gloating, looting and cutting off fugitives 'in the day of their disaster'. Psalm 137, Lamentations and Ezekiel bring the same charge, 1 Esdras says the Edomites burned the temple, and letters from the fort at Arad show Judah's soldiers watching for an Edomite attack.
body: Obadiah's charges are specific: Edom 'stood aloof while strangers carried off his wealth', entered the gate, looted, and stood 'at the crossroads to cut off their fugitives' (verses 11-14). Psalm 137:7 remembers 'the sons of Edom on the day Jerusalem fell: Destroy it … tear it down to its foundations!' Lamentations 4:21-22 and Ezekiel 25:12 and 35:5 say the same.

1 Esdras, in Zerubbabel's speech to Darius, goes further: 'You also vowed to build the temple which the Edomites burned when Judea was made desolate by the Chaldeans' (4:45), and asks that 'the Edomites should give up the villages of the Jews which they held' (4:50). By then Edom had moved into southern Judah, the region later called Idumea.
The ostraca from Arad, a Judahite fort in the Negev, include letters from the last years before the fall that order troops moved because of fears about Edomites nearby.

Obadiah does not date itself. Keil and Delitzsch place it under Jehoram, when Edom revolted (2 Kings 8:20-22) and Philistines and Arabians plundered Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 21:16-17). Emil Hirsch and George Barton, in the Jewish Encyclopedia (1905), take verses 11-14 to describe Nebuchadnezzar's destruction of Jerusalem in 586 BC.

title: Paul quoting the Greek poets
summary: Three times Paul quotes Greek verse: Aratus's 'we are his offspring' at Athens, 'Cretans are always liars' from a Cretan 'prophet', and 'bad company corrupts good character', a line of comedy. Clement of Alexandria, Jerome and Socrates of Constantinople traced each to its source.
body: At Athens: 'As some of your own poets have said, We are His offspring' (Acts 17:28). The words open Aratus's Phaenomena, an astronomical poem of the third century BC: 'From Zeus let us begin … always we all have need of Zeus. For we are also his offspring.' Paul applies to the God he proclaims a line written of Zeus.

To Titus, on Crete: 'As one of their own prophets has said, Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy gluttons' (1:12). Clement of Alexandria and Jerome name the prophet as Epimenides of Crete, the sixth-century BC seer. The first half-line is also in Callimachus's Hymn to Zeus, where the Cretans lie in claiming Zeus's tomb: 'O Lord, for thee the Cretans builded; but thou didst not die, for thou art for ever.' Paul adds, 'This testimony is true.'

To Corinth: 'Bad company corrupts good character' (1 Corinthians 15:33), a line of Greek iambic verse. Jerome says Paul 'quotes a line of Menander', the comic playwright; Socrates of Constantinople credited it to Euripides.
Jerome cites all three to show that Paul knew Greek literature and used it.

title: Where was Paul when he wrote Philippians?
summary: Paul writes Philippians in chains, known to 'the whole palace guard' (the praetorium) and greeted by 'the household of Caesar'. Rome is the traditional answer, but a praetorium and Caesar's slaves existed in provincial capitals too, and Acts itself has Paul kept 'in Herod's Praetorium' at Caesarea.
body: Philippians gives clues but no place. Paul is a prisoner awaiting a verdict that could mean death (1:20-23); his chains are known 'throughout the whole praetorium' (1:13, BSB 'palace guard'); 'those from the household of Caesar' send greetings (4:22); and he hopes to visit Philippi soon (2:24).

Read with Acts 28, Rome is the traditional answer, as in Lightfoot: Paul spent two years there under guard, and the praetorian guard and the emperor's household of slaves and freedmen were in the city.

But praetorium was also the word for a governor's headquarters anywhere: the Gospels use it of Pilate's in Jerusalem (Mark 15:16, John 18:28), and Acts 23:35 has Paul held 'in Herod's Praetorium' at Caesarea for two years. 'Caesar's household' included imperial slaves and freedmen across the provinces. Gerald Hawthorne argues for Caesarea. G. S. Duncan argues for Ephesus, where Paul says he 'fought wild beasts' (1 Corinthians 15:32) and 'despaired even of life' (2 Corinthians 1:8), though Acts records no imprisonment there; Ephesus, being nearer Philippi, would make the several journeys the letter implies easier.
The answer changes the date — on a chronology counted from the Gallio date, ≈mid-50s from Ephesus, ≈late 50s from Caesarea, ≈early 60s from Rome — and so where the letter falls among Paul's others.

title: A beating instead of death, or before it
summary: Rome beat people for three purposes: as a penalty in its own right, to question them, and as the first part of an execution. Pilate offers the first: 'I will punish Him and release Him' (Luke 23:16, 22). Mark and Matthew record the third: Jesus flogged and 'handed over to be crucified' (Mark 15:15). Livy and Josephus record others flogged before they were crucified.
body: A beating could stand alone. The Digest of Roman law lists beating with rods among the penalties that touch a man's standing 'and not the danger of his life' (48.19.28.1), and Acts shows the other uses: magistrates have Paul and Silas 'beaten with rods' and then let them go (Acts 16:22, 35), and a commander orders Paul 'flogged and interrogated' to find out what he had done (22:24).

A beating also came before crucifixion. Livy records that after a slave revolt in Etruria in 196 BC the praetor had its leaders 'flogged and fixed to crosses' (verberatos crucibus adfixit). Josephus says the governor Florus had men 'whipped and nailed to the cross before his tribunal' in Jerusalem in AD 66, and that men caught during Titus' siege 'were first whipped, and then tormented… and were then crucified'. Sherwin-White sets the scourging (verbera) among the beatings as the one joined to a capital sentence.

In Luke Pilate twice proposes to 'punish' Jesus (paideusas, the word for disciplining a child) and release Him, a beating instead of a death sentence. In John, Pilate has Jesus flogged (emastigōsen) in the middle of the trial, before any sentence, and brings Him out in the thorns and purple: 'Here is the man!' (John 19:1–5). The chief priests and officers answer, 'Crucify Him! Crucify Him!' (19:6). Mark and Matthew place the flogging (phragellōsas, from the Latin flagellum) after the sentence, as the start of the execution.

A. N. Sherwin-White, a Roman historian, drew a scale of three beatings (fustes, rods; flagella, whips; verbera, the scourging joined to a capital sentence) from a list in the Digest (48.19.7: 'fustium admonitio, flagellorum castigatio, vinculorum verberatio'). The list is a third-century jurist's, Callistratus's. Whether the Gospels tell of one beating, which John places in the middle of the trial, or of two, a lighter one in John and the scourging before crucifixion in Mark and Matthew, is read both ways.

title: What the first witnesses suffered, as the sources tell it
summary: Paul's list of those the risen Jesus appeared to names Cephas, the Twelve, James and Paul himself. The New Testament, Josephus and 1 Clement record the violent deaths of four of them: James son of Zebedee, James the Lord's brother, Peter and Paul.
body: Paul passes on a list he says he 'received' (1 Corinthians 15:3-8): Jesus 'appeared to Cephas and then to the Twelve', then to more than five hundred, 'most of whom are still living', 'then to James, then to all the apostles', and last of all to Paul. He wrote from Ephesus (16:8). Against those in Corinth who said 'there is no resurrection of the dead' (15:12), he sets out what would follow if they were right: Christ was not raised, and 'we are also exposed as false witnesses about God' (15:15). He answers, 'But Christ has indeed been raised from the dead' (15:20).

Acts has Peter and John arrested while 'proclaiming in Jesus the resurrection of the dead' (4:2), ordered to stop, and answering, 'we cannot stop speaking about what we have seen and heard' (4:20). Flogged later, the apostles 'did not stop teaching and proclaiming the good news that Jesus is the Christ' (5:40-42). Paul lists imprisonments, five times the forty lashes minus one, and a stoning (2 Corinthians 11:23-27), writes that God has displayed the apostles 'like prisoners appointed for death' (1 Corinthians 4:9), and ties the danger to the resurrection: 'why do we endanger ourselves every hour?' … 'If the dead are not raised, “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.”' (15:30-32).

Four of those the list names have violent deaths recorded in the New Testament, Josephus or 1 Clement. James son of Zebedee, one of the Twelve, was put to death 'with the sword' (Acts 12:2). James the Lord's brother was stoned in AD 62 (Josephus); Eusebius takes the James of 15:7 to be him, 'one of the so-called brethren of the Saviour'. Peter and Paul 'suffered martyrdom' (1 Clement 5), which does not say where; Dionysius of Corinth (≈AD 170) says it was in Italy, and Tertullian (≈AD 200–210) in Rome under Nero. Each has a card of its own, linked below, as does what is told of the rest of the Twelve.

Two of the four had not been followers. Jesus' brothers, James among them (Mark 6:3), 'did not believe in Him' (John 7:5), and Paul had 'persecuted the church of God and tried to destroy it' (Galatians 1:13).

None of these sources records any of the four being offered his life for a denial. Tacitus describes Nero's victims as convicted in great numbers and says nothing of pardon (Annals 15.44); the release of Christians who denied the name is recorded by Pliny in Bithynia, ≈AD 110–112. Whether any of them recanted is taken up by the argument in the linked card.

title: 'Would they die for a lie?' The argument from the apostles' suffering
summary: Christian apologists from William Paley (1794) to Sean McDowell (2015) argue that the first witnesses suffered and died rather than abandon their claim to have seen Jesus risen, and so were not inventing it. McDowell limits the argument to their sincerity, not the truth of what they believed; Bart Ehrman, who explains the appearances as visions, also holds that they were not inventing them.
body: William Paley set the argument out in 1794 as the first proposition of his Evidences of Christianity: 'That there is satisfactory evidence that many professing to be original witnesses of the Christian miracles passed their lives in labours, dangers, and sufferings, voluntarily undergone in attestation of the accounts which they delivered, and solely in consequence of their belief of those accounts.' His second is that there is not satisfactory evidence that witnesses to other miracles have acted in the same manner.

Sean McDowell, who weighed the evidence for each apostle's death (2015), rates the martyrdom of Peter, Paul, James son of Zebedee and James the Lord's brother at the 'highest possible probability' on his scale. He states the argument's limits himself: the apostles' willingness to die 'does not demonstrate "the inherent truth of the Christian message," but that the apostles really believed that Jesus had risen from the grave'; 'The apostles could have been mistaken, but their willingness to die as martyrs establishes their unmistakable sincerity.' On recanting he writes, 'While there are no early accounts that any of the apostles recanted, we simply don't know how many of them were killed for their testimony about Christ.'

Bart Ehrman, a historian who explains the appearances as visions rather than a bodily resurrection, also holds the witnesses sincere. He said in 2014: 'the historical reality appears to be that Christianity was not invented by people with an ulterior purpose … It originated in real, actual experiences of some of Jesus' followers, as they had visions of Jesus not long after his death.'

title: James son of Zebedee, put to death by Herod
summary: Acts gives it one sentence: Herod 'had James, the brother of John, put to death with the sword'. It was between AD 41 and 44, and apart from Judas's it is the only death of one of the Twelve that the New Testament tells.
body: Acts 12:1-3 sets the death under 'King Herod', Herod Agrippa I, who seized Peter next and died soon after at Caesarea (12:19-23). He ruled Judea from AD 41, and Josephus puts his death in the seventh year of his reign, AD 44, so the death of James falls between the two. James was one of the three Jesus took apart with him, with Peter and John (Mark 5:37; 9:2; 14:33).
Acts gives no charge, no trial and no offer to recant.

When James and John asked for the places at his right and left, Jesus told them, 'You will drink the cup that I drink' (Mark 10:39). Clement of Alexandria, ≈AD 200, passed on a story he had 'from those who had lived before him': the man who brought James to court was moved by his testimony, declared himself a Christian too, asked James's forgiveness on the way, and the two 'were both beheaded at the same time'. Eusebius preserves it; no earlier source tells it.

title: What the early sources say of Peter's death
summary: John's Gospel says Jesus foretold 'the kind of death by which Peter would glorify God'. 1 Clement says Peter 'suffered martyrdom'; Dionysius of Corinth (≈AD 170) puts it in Italy, Tertullian (≈AD 200–210) on a cross in Rome under Nero, and Gaius (≈AD 200) points to his 'trophy' on the Vatican hill. Otto Zwierlein (2009) argues that none of the sources placing it in Rome rests on knowledge of the event.
body: John 21:18-19: 'when you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and someone else will dress you and lead you where you do not want to go.' 'Jesus said this to indicate the kind of death by which Peter would glorify God.' 2 Peter has him say 'this tent will soon be laid aside, as our Lord Jesus Christ has made clear to me' (1:14). 1 Peter sends greetings from 'the church in Babylon' (5:13); Eusebius reports Clement of Alexandria and Papias as saying the letter was written 'in Rome itself', the city called Babylon 'by a figure'.

1 Clement, sent in the name of the church of Rome to Corinth (Eusebius places Clement as its bishop from Domitian's twelfth year to Trajan's third, ≈AD 92–100 reckoned from their accessions), holds up Peter and Paul as 'the noble examples furnished in our own generation': Peter 'endured not one or two, but numerous labours; and when he had at length suffered martyrdom, departed to the place of glory due to him'. It does not say where or how. The letter to the Romans that bears the name of Ignatius of Antioch, whom Eusebius has taken to Rome under Trajan (AD 98–117), says: 'I do not, as Peter and Paul, issue commandments unto you.'

About AD 170 Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, wrote to Rome that Peter and Paul 'taught together in like manner in Italy, and suffered martyrdom at the same time'. Tertullian, ≈AD 200, writes that at Rome 'Peter endures a passion like his Lord's', and ≈AD 210, quoting John 21:18: 'At Rome Nero was the first who stained with blood the rising faith. Then is Peter girt by another, when he is made fast to the cross.' Origen, as Eusebius reports him, says Peter 'was crucified head-downwards; for he had requested that he might suffer in this way'.

Gaius, a Roman churchman in the time of bishop Zephyrinus (198–217, as Guarducci dates him), told an opponent: 'if you will go to the Vatican or to the Ostian way, you will find the trophies of those who laid the foundations of this church.' Excavations under St Peter's Basilica in 1939–49 found a small shrine (an aedicula) built against a red-plastered wall in a cemetery on the Vatican hill. The wall is dated ≈AD 160 by five tiles over a drain beside it, stamped with the names of Aurelius Caesar and Faustina, a pairing used between 146 and 161. Margherita Guarducci, writing on the excavations in 1960, says 'virtually all scholars admit' the shrine is the trophy Gaius names.

Otto Zwierlein (2009) argues that Peter 'never visited Rome, did not undergo martyrdom there, was not buried there', as his reviewer Pieter van der Horst summarises it. On his reading 'Babylon' in 1 Peter 5:13 is the diaspora of 1:1, not Rome; 1 Clement knows nothing of Peter beyond Acts and dates from the 120s; the letters of Ignatius are spurious and late second century; and the first sources to place Peter's death in Rome, from Dionysius on, all come from the last decades of the second century.

title: What the early sources say of Paul's death
summary: Acts ends with Paul two years in Rome, still preaching. 1 Clement says he 'suffered martyrdom under the prefects'; Tertullian (≈AD 200–210) puts his death in Rome under Nero, and Eusebius says he was beheaded there.
body: Acts and the letters speak of the danger: 'in town after town the Holy Spirit warns me that chains and afflictions await me' (Acts 20:23); 'Christ will be exalted in my body, whether by life or by death' (Philippians 1:20); and 2 Timothy has him write, 'I am already being poured out like a drink offering, and the time of my departure is at hand' (4:6). Acts closes with him two years in Rome, where 'boldly and freely he proclaimed the kingdom of God' (28:31), and does not say what came next.

1 Clement: Paul, 'after being seven times thrown into captivity, compelled to flee, and stoned', had 'come to the extreme limit of the west, and suffered martyrdom under the prefects'. It does not name the place. Polycarp of Smyrna, writing to Philippi after Ignatius had passed through (ch. 13), sets 'Paul himself, and the rest of the apostles' beside Ignatius as those now with the Lord, 'with whom also they suffered. For they loved not this present world, but Him who died for us, and for our sakes was raised again by God from the dead.'

Tertullian, ≈AD 200, writes that at Rome 'Paul wins his crown in a death like John's', and ≈AD 210 that there 'Paul obtain[s] a birth suited to Roman citizenship'. Paul was a citizen (Acts 22:25-28). Eusebius writes that 'Paul was beheaded in Rome itself'. He introduces Gaius's 'trophies' at the Vatican and on the Ostian way as 'the places where the sacred corpses of the aforesaid apostles are laid'; Guarducci reads them as Peter's and Paul's respectively, and the basilica of St Paul Outside the Walls stands on the Ostian way.
Paul writes that he had 'persecuted the church of God and tried to destroy it' (Galatians 1:13), and that the risen Jesus 'appeared to me also' (1 Corinthians 15:8).

title: What the early sources say of the other apostles' deaths
summary: For the Twelve beyond Peter, James son of Zebedee and Judas, the sources gathered here date from the late second century on. Polycrates of Ephesus says John and Philip lie buried in Asia, and Heracleon (≈AD 170–180), as George Salmon reads him, names Matthew, Philip and Thomas among those never called to confess before the authorities.
body: John 21:23 corrects 'the rumor … that this disciple would not die'. Irenaeus, ≈AD 180, says John remained at Ephesus 'permanently until the times of Trajan' (AD 98–117). Polycrates, bishop of Ephesus, writing to Victor of Rome, says John 'sleeps at Ephesus' and that 'Philip, one of the twelve apostles … sleeps in Hierapolis'. Tertullian, ≈AD 200, tells that John was 'plunged, unhurt, into boiling oil, and thence remitted to his island-exile'. A different report is credited to Papias: as Henry Cowan summarises it, the chronicler George Hamartolos (ninth century) quotes his second book as saying that John 'was put to death by the Jews', and an epitome of Philip of Side makes a similar quotation.

Origen, as Eusebius reports him, says where some of them went: 'Parthia, according to tradition, was allotted to Thomas as his field of labor, Scythia to Andrew, and Asia to John'. The apocryphal Acts of Andrew, which M. R. James dates to the third century, tell of Andrew crucified at Patrae by the proconsul Aegeates; the Acts of Thomas tell of Thomas taken up a mountain in India on King Misdaeus's order and pierced by four soldiers with spears.

Heracleon, a Valentinian teacher quoted by Clement of Alexandria, distinguishes confession in one's life from confession by the voice before the authorities, and goes on: 'Of whom are Matthew, Philip, Thomas, Levi, and many others.' Which kind the list belongs to turns on the sentence before it, which the New Advent translation gives as 'all the saved have confessed with the confession made by the voice, and departed'; George Salmon reads Heracleon as naming those who 'have never been called on to make it'. Clement, answering him, says Heracleon 'seems to be of the same sentiments with us in this section'.

Sean McDowell (2015), weighing each case, rates the martyrdom of Thomas 'more probable than not', of Andrew 'more plausible than not', of the other apostles 'as plausible as not', and of John 'improbable'.
